The open source ones have many advantages, an army of people working on it from many companies, governments and individuals, it also doesn't have the issue of privacy or security, being that it's open source and can run locally on your home PC, it makes it a lot more transparent.

But the biggest advantage the open source ones have, is that no one controls it, rivals to any A.I. company that doesn't want to build their own or can't, it makes sense for them to help the open source community to build A.I. systems that anyone can use, and that's the key, A.I. is going to be so important to the world economy, hardly any governments or rival corporations are going to want a few governments and companies controlling the vast bulk of A.I. and open source gets around that by decentralising it.

The irony is about OpenAI, that the biggest downfall could be that they've become closedAI and are becoming too greedy so early on when we are seeing clear signs that other alternatives can deliver the goods for far less money.

I have to admit, early on in this year, there was a lot of excitement about the online A.I. models, but as time went on, and we've seen the games and restrictions the companies have put on their services, the open source models look a lot more appealing on many fronts, being open and transparent, no trust issues or restrictions and can also run locally on your PC.

Early this year, I didn't think it was possible to get a good chatbot running on your PC, but with how rapidly open source A.I. is developing, I'm surprised at the quality it's already delivering, and we are still at the early stage, you can only imagine how much better it's going to get over the next year, 5 years and so on.

For now, the only drawback open source models have when running locally, they really need to sort out the mess of what system it can run on, most of the time it's Nvidia only or cpu only, for open source A.I. to really take off, it needs to just work on AMD, Intel, Nvidia, ARM's and cpu as a fallback, they also need to clean up the installation process, as it's a bit of a mess at the moment, also, a nice and clean interface would go along way with getting adoption.

A lot of those problems could be resolved this year, but until they are, for now, it's just easier for most consumers to use online models.

comments.text:
They are somewhat wrong here actually, even though I hate to say it. While open source is huge and incredibly important, you could have said all the same things about linux around year 2000. There was a very strong sense that open source would take over everything including the desktop. While it ate unix for lunch, and took over web-hosting, it never really went anywhere else outside of a few exceptions. Why? Because open source is great at providing building blocks, but terrible at delivering packaged solutions to personal and business problems and making industry partnerships. All of that esoteric hardware from plotters to xray machines to every industry specific line of business software like AutoCAD, dental scheduling, Photoshop, etc, none of that came over, it's still all on windows, and apple has the music industry and some of the graphics stuff.

Similarly, while the building blocks of AI will be publicly accessible, the integration of AI with business applications and data will still be provided by the same players. I bloody hate MS's ecosystem, Azure is a rats nest and I've genuinely been surprised how readily businesses are jumping into that dumpster fire. however because of their continued monopoly of the desktop and increasing control over the enterprise ecosystem through o360 & azure it actually puts them in the perfect position to dominate AI solutions both on the desktop and in business data. Say for example you're a law firm storing all of your case documents and files in onedrive/sharepoint/dynamics. Last year I would have said you're insane, they are massively expensive and just... oh man.  but now say you can ask your computer verbally to "Look through all my companies files and emails and give me a report on any situation where Mr X discussed Topic Y with anyone from Company Z"  well now you have just changed everything and put legions of paralegals out of work (or significantly changed their work at least). Meta.... what do they have really? A popular website that is fundamentally disposable. If facebook vanished tomorrow nothing really changes, the marketing and networking goes somewhere else, but it doesn't matter, it wouldn't really be very painful. Google has search, and their few other services work very well, but they don't have the kind of deep reach and integration into businesses that Microsoft does.

So yeah, as much as I hate to admit it, MS is really in the best position by far. The future is as clear as day. They have the massive client list already. And they happen to be on the leading edge of it for the first time in two decades. As idiotic as they are sometimes, I literally can't imagine how they could mess this up. Or rather, they definitely will mess it up, and it will be a huge pain in the ass for us that have to integrate and support it, but they still will somehow dominate everyone else despite that as usual.

But what you won't see are individual people and companies abandoning the big companies for free software extolling liberty and singing kumbaya. I would be thrilled to be wrong about that, but I'm not going to be.
